The ground here moves more than most of Melbourne<\/h3>

Melbourne's western suburbs sit on reactive clay<\/strong> \u2014 flat volcanic ground classified from Class M up to Class H under AS 2870, the Australian standard for slabs on reactive soils. The higher the class, the more the ground moves.<\/p>

Wet winters, dry summers, a slab caught in between<\/h3>

Reactive clay swells when it's wet and shrinks when it dries. Across a Melbourne year of wet winters and dry summers, that means the ground under your driveway is constantly rising and falling. A slab that wasn't built to handle that movement gets flexed every season until it cracks. It's why a driveway that would sit flat for decades in sandy soil can crack within a few years out here \u2014 the concrete isn't worse, the ground is working against it.<\/p>

Most cracked driveways failed at the base, not the surface<\/h3>

The mix is rarely the problem. The problem is a slab laid on moving ground without the preparation that lets it cope \u2014 which is why we spend the time on the sub-base, the reinforcement height and the drainage rather than rushing to the pour. If you want the full explanation, we've written a guide on why concrete cracks and how the base controls A driveway isn't a path with cars on it \u2014 it carries vehicle loads over moving ground, and the spec has to match that:<\/p>\n \n

    \n
  • Slab thickness.<\/strong> A standard residential driveway is around 100mm<\/strong>. Thinner slabs don't have the strength to bridge ground movement and vehicle loads at the same time.<\/li>\n
  • Reinforcement.<\/strong> Steel mesh \u2014 commonly SL72<\/strong> for a residential driveway \u2014 held up on bar chairs so it sits within<\/em> the slab. Mesh lying on the dirt does almost nothing.<\/li>\n
  • Heavier loads.<\/strong> Caravans, boats, trucks or steep access get increased thickness and heavier reinforcement, sized at the quote.<\/li>\n
  • The sub-base.<\/strong> A compacted crushed-rock base under the slab, so the concrete sits on uniform support instead of soft spots that settle or fill that heaves.<\/li>\n
  • Concrete strength.<\/strong> Specified in MPa (typically 20\u201332 MPa) to suit the job.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n \n

    We size the thickness, mesh and mix at the on-site quote rather than pouring a generic spec and hoping. If your driveway needs to take a caravan or sits on a slope, it gets built for     1. Site prep & excavation<\/strong> \u2014 clear the area, set levels, dig to the right depth.<\/li>
    2. Base & compaction<\/strong> \u2014 crushed-rock base, properly compacted so nothing shifts later.<\/li>
    3. Formwork & steel<\/strong> \u2014 form the edges, lay reinforcing mesh or bar sized to the load, held on bar chairs.<\/li>
    4. Pour & finish<\/strong> \u2014 pour, screed level, and apply your chosen finish (broom, exposed, coloured).<\/li>

item.content:encoded:
Concreters Werribee

From new estates to established homes, we install and replace concrete driveways, crossovers, exposed aggregate, slabs, paths and patios throughout Werribee, with proper site preparation, reinforcement and fixed-price quotes.

Get Your FREE Quote Today Call us - 03 4427 9541

Our Services

Whatever the pour, we match you with concreters who do it every week.

Concrete Driveways

New driveways, replacements, crossovers

Exposed Aggregate

The premium textured, non-slip finish with real kerb appeal.

Concrete Slabs

Shed, garage, extension and house slabs fitted properly for your needs

Paths & Pathways

Footpaths, side access, garden paths

Patios & Alfresco

Outdoor entertaining areas

Coloured & Decorative

Coloured, stencil, honed finishes

Concreting for Werribee's two kinds of home

Werribee isn't a single-era suburb like the newer estates around it. As the oldest and largest centre in Wyndham, it has two distinct kinds of concreting work, and they need different approaches.

Established homes — the brick-veneer streets

Werribee's older streets are lined with the classic orange and cream brick-veneer homes built through the 1950s, 60s, 70s and 80s. The concrete on these properties is now decades old — original driveways and paths that have cracked, lifted and become trip hazards, often poured on bases that were never built for how much the local clay moves. Here the work is usually driveway replacement: breaking out the old slab, checking what's underneath, matching the existing garage and footpath levels, and repouring on a base that actually handles the ground.

New estates — Riverwalk, Harpley and the growth corridor

On the other side of the suburb, estates like Riverwalk and Harpley are still being built out with brand-new homes needing driveways, shed and garage slabs, paths and outdoor areas poured from scratch. On these lots the ground has usually been cut, filled and compacted by the building trades before the driveway stage — so the sub-base needs checking rather than assuming it's sound, especially over fill.

Werribee's reactive clay and the Werribee River

Werribee sits on the flat volcanic plains of Melbourne's west, on reactive clay classified Class M to Class H under AS 2870 — ground that swells when wet and shrinks when it dries, moving beneath a slab through the seasons. It's the single biggest reason concrete cracks out here, and it's why base preparation matters more in Werribee than in most of Melbourne. If you want the full explanation, we've written a guide on why concrete cracks on this ground.

The Werribee River winding through the suburb adds a local wrinkle: properties closer to the river and the low-lying areas need particular attention to drainage and finished levels, because water that collects against a slab drives the exact moisture swings that heave and crack it. Before we quote, we look at how water actually moves across your site — not just where the concrete goes, but where the water needs to go.

How we prepare the ground in Werribee

Ground conditions vary across Werribee. Established blocks often have clay-based natural ground; newer estate homes can have disturbed soil or areas of fill left from construction. Soft or unsuitable material needs to be identified before concrete goes down, not covered over and hoped for.

Where needed, the area is excavated and prepared with a properly compacted crushed-rock base before formwork and reinforcement go in. That preparation matters most beneath driveways, garage approaches and slabs that carry vehicles. Reinforcement — steel mesh held up on bar chairs so it sits within the slab, not on the dirt — and the right slab thickness are what let the concrete bridge the ground movement instead of cracking through it.

Drainage, levels and crack control

The finished level of the concrete matters as much as the colour or finish. A slab needs to be set out so water runs away from the home, garage and fences instead of pooling along walls and slab edges — and existing garage floors, door thresholds, paths and neighbouring surfaces all have to be worked in when setting the falls.

Concrete also contracts as it cures and keeps moving with temperature and ground moisture. Reinforcement holds a slab together but doesn't make it crack-proof — nothing does. That's what control joints are for: planned lines, cut to about a quarter of the slab's depth, that give shrinkage somewhere tidy to go instead of cracking randomly across the surface. We place them around internal corners, garage entrances, changes in slab width and where new concrete meets old.

Council crossovers in Werribee

Any new driveway that meets the road needs a council-approved vehicle crossover before it's poured. In Werribee that's Wyndham City Council consent — it sits on council land, comes with a fee and a lead time, and has to be plain concrete where there's a footpath, so a decorative driveway finish stops at the boundary. On an older Werribee home, if you're replacing the driveway it's the natural time to redo an aging crossover too. We handle the consent as part of the job so you're not chasing council yourself.

WHY CUSTOMERS CHOOSE US

Groundwork done properly — compacted base and correct reinforcement, not a fast pour.

Insured Concreters

Workmanship You Can Rely On

Workmanship guarantee

AREAS WE COVER AROUND WERRIBEE

We service Werribee and the surrounding Wyndham suburbs, including Werribee South, Wyndham Vale, Hoppers Crossing, Point Cook, Tarneit and Truganina.

Planning Concrete Work in Werribee?

FAQ

Do you service Werribee?

Yes — Werribee is one of our core areas. We cover Werribee and the surrounding Wyndham suburbs for driveways, slabs, exposed aggregate, paths and patios.

Do I need council approval for a driveway crossover in Werribee?

A new vehicle crossover onto the road generally needs approval from Wyndham City Council; a driveway on your own property often doesn’t. We’ll point you to the right requirements before we start. Check out our Guide

How much does a concrete driveway cost in Werribee?


It depends on size, finish and access — plain concrete is the most affordable, exposed aggregate and decorative finishes cost more. We give a free on-site fixed-price quote.

Werribee isn't a single-era suburb like the newer estates around it. As the oldest and largest centre in Wyndham, it has two distinct kinds of concreting work, and they need different approaches.<\/p>\n \n

Established homes \u2014 the brick-veneer streets<\/h3>\n

Werribee's older streets are lined with the classic orange and cream brick-veneer homes built through the 1950s, 60s, 70s and 80s. The concrete on these properties is now decades old \u2014 original driveways and paths that have cracked, lifted and become trip hazards, often poured on bases that were never built for how much the local clay moves. Here the work is usually driveway replacement<\/a>: breaking out the old slab, checking what's underneath, matching the existing garage and footpath levels, and repouring on a base that actually handles the ground.<\/p>\n \n

New estates \u2014 Riverwalk, Harpley and the growth corridor<\/h3>\n

On the other side of the suburb, estates like Riverwalk and Harpley are still being built out with brand-new homes needing driveways, shed and garage slabs<\/a>, paths<\/a> and outdoor areas poured from scratch. On these lots the ground has usually been cut, filled and compacted by the building trades before the driveway stage \u2014 so the sub-base needs checking rather than assuming it's sound, especially over fill.<\/p>","align":"center","typography_typography":"custom","typography_font_family":"Poppins","typography_font_weight":"400","__globals__":{"text_color":"globals\/colors?id=astglobalcolor2"}},"elements":[],"widgetType":"text-editor"}],"isInner":false}],"isInner":false,"styles":{"e-59113f6":{"id":"e-59113f6","label":"local","type":"class","variants":[{"meta":{"breakpoint":"desktop","state":null},"props":{"flex-direction":{"$$type":"string","value":"column"}},"custom_css":null}]}},"interactions":[],"editor_settings":[],"version":"0.0"},{"id":"40d980a","elType":"container","settings":{"container_type":"grid","grid_columns_grid":{"unit":"fr","size":"2"},"grid_rows_grid":{"unit":"fr","size":"1"},"grid_rows_grid_mobile":{"unit":"fr","size":"1"}},"elements":[{"id":"b3854cc","elType":"container","settings":{"content_width":"full"},"elements":[{"id":"9d20975","elType":"widget","settings":{"classes":{"$$type":"classes","value":["e-9d20975-690f059"]},"title":{"$$type":"html-v3","value":{"content":{"$$type":"string","value":"Werribee's reactive clay and the Werribee River"},"children":[]}},"link":{"$$type":"link","value":{"isTargetBlank":null}}},"elements":[],"widgetType":"e-heading","styles":{"e-9d20975-690f059":{"id":"e-9d20975-690f059","label":"local","type":"class","variants":[{"meta":{"breakpoint":"desktop","state":null},"props":{"font-family":{"$$type":"font-family","value":"Poppins"},"font-weight":{"$$type":"string","value":"400"},"font-size":{"$$type":"size","value":{"size":30,"unit":"px"}},"text-align":{"$$type":"string","value":"center"}},"custom_css":null}]}},"interactions":[],"editor_settings":[],"version":"0.0"},{"id":"4e05a36","elType":"widget","settings":{"editor":"

Werribee sits on the flat volcanic plains of Melbourne's west, on reactive clay<\/strong> classified Class M to Class H under AS 2870 \u2014 ground that swells when wet and shrinks when it dries, moving beneath a slab through the seasons. It's the single biggest reason concrete cracks out here, and it's why base preparation matters more in Werribee than in most of Melbourne. If you want the full explanation, we've written a guide on why concrete cracks on this ground<\/a>.<\/p>\n \n

The Werribee River winding through the suburb adds a local wrinkle: properties closer to the river and the low-lying areas need particular attention to drainage and finished levels, because water that collects against a slab drives the exact moisture swings that heave and crack it. Before we quote, we look at how water actually moves across your site \u2014 not just where the concrete goes, but where the water needs to Ground conditions vary across Werribee. Established blocks often have clay-based natural ground; newer estate homes can have disturbed soil or areas of fill left from construction. Soft or unsuitable material needs to be identified before concrete goes down, not covered over and hoped for.<\/p>\n \n

Where needed, the area is excavated and prepared with a properly compacted crushed-rock base before formwork and reinforcement go in. That preparation matters most beneath driveways, garage approaches and slabs that carry vehicles. Reinforcement \u2014 steel mesh held up on bar chairs so it sits within the slab, not on the dirt \u2014 and the right slab thickness are what let the concrete bridge the ground movement instead of cracking through it.<\/p>","align":"center","typography_typography":"custom","typography_font_family":"Poppins","typography_font_weight":"400","__globals__":{"text_color":"globals\/colors?id=astglobalcolor2"}},"elements":[],"widgetType":"text-editor"}],"isInner":true}],"isInner":true}],"isInner":false},{"id":"8d1059a","elType":"e-flexbox","settings":{"classes":{"$$type":"classes","value":["e-2169a80"]}},"elements":[{"id":"b5b5a5c","elType":"container","settings":{"container_type":"grid","grid_columns_grid":{"unit":"fr","size":"2"},"grid_rows_grid":{"unit":"fr","size":"1"},"grid_rows_grid_mobile":{"unit":"fr","size":"1"}},"elements":[{"id":"9075379","elType":"container","settings":{"content_width":"full"},"elements":[{"id":"f927f1b","elType":"widget","settings":{"classes":{"$$type":"classes","value":["e-f927f1b-e1222b1"]},"title":{"$$type":"html-v3","value":{"content":{"$$type":"string","value":"Drainage, levels and crack control"},"children":[]}},"link":{"$$type":"link","value":{"isTargetBlank":null}}},"elements":[],"widgetType":"e-heading","styles":{"e-f927f1b-e1222b1":{"id":"e-f927f1b-e1222b1","label":"local","type":"class","variants":[{"meta":{"breakpoint":"desktop","state":null},"props":{"font-family":{"$$type":"font-family","value":"Poppins"},"font-weight":{"$$type":"string","value":"400"},"font-size":{"$$type":"size","value":{"size":30,"unit":"px"}},"text-align":{"$$type":"string","value":"center"}},"custom_css":null}]}},"interactions":[],"editor_settings":[],"version":"0.0"},{"id":"2c02c74","elType":"widget","settings":{"editor":"

The finished level of the concrete matters as much as the colour or finish. A slab needs to be set out so water runs away from the home, garage and fences instead of pooling along walls and slab edges \u2014 and existing garage floors, door thresholds, paths and neighbouring surfaces all have to be worked in when setting the falls.<\/p>\n \n

Concrete also contracts as it cures and keeps moving with temperature and ground moisture. Reinforcement holds a slab together but doesn't make it crack-proof \u2014 nothing does. That's what control joints are for: planned lines, cut to about a quarter of the slab's depth, that give shrinkage somewhere tidy to go instead of cracking randomly across the surface. We place them around internal corners, garage entrances, changes in slab width and where new concrete meets On an older Werribee home, if you're replacing the driveway it's the natural time to redo an aging crossover too. item.title: Concrete driveway cost per m2 melbourne
item.dc:creator: Admin-iU1Tj
item.content:encoded:
Concrete Driveway Cost Per m² in Melbourne (2026 Guide)

Short answer: In Melbourne, a plain concrete driveway typically costs $70–$130 per square metre, and decorative finishes like exposed aggregate, coloured or stencilled concrete run $100–$200+ per square metre. For a typical 40m² driveway, that's roughly $3,000–$5,500 plain, or $4,500–$8,000+ for exposed aggregate.

If you've searched this before, you've probably noticed the numbers never match. That's not because anyone's lying — it's because the per-m² rate is only half the story. Below is what actually sits behind those numbers, and why two quotes for the same driveway can differ by thousands.

WHY YOU'LL SEE DIFFERENT PRICES ONLINE

Search "concrete driveway cost per m² Melbourne" and you'll find figures from $70 to $180 per square metre. All of them can be right, because a per-m² rate can either:

  • Include only the pour — the concrete, labour and finish, on a flat, easy, already-prepared site; or
  • Include the whole job — excavation, removal of the old driveway, crushed-rock base, reinforcement, formwork, control joints, drainage and sealing.

The first number looks cheaper and isn't comparable. When you're comparing quotes, the question that matters isn't "what's your per-m² rate" — it's "what's included at that rate?"

CONCRETE DRIVEWAY COST PER m² BY FINISH

Melbourne market ranges, 2026:

FinishCost per m²40m² driveway (typical)
Plain concrete$70 – $130$2,800 – $5,200
Coloured concrete$75 – $130$3,000 – $5,200
Exposed aggregate$100 – $180$4,000 – $7,200
Stencilled / stamped$100 – $200$4,000 – $8,000
Honed / polished$150 – $200+$6,000 – $8,000+

Decorative finishes typically add 20–80% over plain concrete, depending on the technique. Exposed aggregate — the most popular premium finish — usually sits around 40–60% above plain, reflecting the extra labour to wash back the surface at exactly the right moment in the cure, plus sealing.

Worth knowing: the premium buys appearance and grip, not lifespan. A well-laid plain driveway and a well-laid exposed aggregate driveway both last roughly 25–40 years. You're paying for how it looks and how it grips underfoot, not for durability.

DRIVEWAY FINISHES EXPLAINED

The finish changes both the price and how the driveway performs underfoot:

- Broom finish

The most common. A broom is drawn across the wet surface to create fine texture, giving traction so the driveway isn't slippery when wet. Cheapest, and genuinely practical.

-Exposed aggregate

The top layer of cement is washed back to reveal the stone. Textured, non-slip, and the most popular premium finish in Melbourne. (link → exposed aggregate page)

-Coloured concrete

Oxide pigment mixed through the concrete for a consistent tone (charcoal, sandstone, terracotta). Adds appearance for a modest premium.

-Stamped / stencilled

Patterns pressed or stencilled into the surface to imitate brick, slate or tile. Adds roughly 30–70% over plain, depending on pattern complexity.

-Stained

Acid or water-based stains applied to the surface for decorative colour effects. Versatile and relatively economical.

-Rock salt finish

Salt is pressed into the wet surface then washed out, leaving a subtly pitted, skid-resistant texture.

-Honed / polished

Ground smooth and sealed for a refined look. Better suited to covered patios and alfresco areas than driveways, for slip reasons.

-Pervious concrete

A porous mix that lets water drain through into the soil beneath. Useful for stormwater management on sites with drainage constraints.

WHAT ACTUALLY MOVES YOUR PRICE

Two driveways of identical size can quote thousands apart. Here's why:

- Site preparation and excavation

The single biggest swing factor. Clearing, digging to depth, and laying a compacted crushed-rock base is real work. A driveway on a difficult site costs materially more than the same driveway on a clean, level one.

-Removing the old driveway

Breaking up and carting away an existing slab adds demolition, labour and tip fees. Ask whether removal is in the quote or priced separately — this is where "cheap" quotes often hide.

-Slope and access

A sloping block typically adds around $10 per m². Tight access — no room for a truck, so concrete has to be pumped or barrowed — adds cost again.

-Thickness and reinforcement

A standard residential driveway is around 100mm thick with reinforcing mesh. If you're parking a caravan, boat or heavy vehicle, you need more thickness and heavier steel. That's not upselling; it's what stops the slab cracking.

-Crossover works and council approval

The crossover — the section from the road to your property boundary — sits on council land and needs consent before anyone pours it. Two costs people miss: the council consent fee, and the crossover works themselves, which are quoted separately from the driveway. Rules and fees vary by council — in Wyndham, consent starts at $102.60. See our guide to Wyndham Council's vehicle crossing requirements for the full fee schedule.

-Drainage and falls

Getting the falls right so water runs away from the house is part of the job, not an extra. Skipping it is how you end up with pooling and, eventually, a damp problem.

-Sealing

Decorative finishes need sealing to protect the surface and hold the colour. Factor in a reseal every few years.

WHERE THE MONEY ACTUALLY GOES

A per-m² figure hides three separate costs. Understanding the split is how you judge whether a quote is fair:

Materials

The single biggest swing factor. Clearing, digging to depth, and laying a compacted crushed-rock base is real work. A driveway on a difficult site costs materially more than the same driveway on a clean, level one.

Labour

Breaking up and carting away an existing slab adds demolition, labour and tip fees. Ask whether removal is in the quote or priced separately — this is where "cheap" quotes often hide.

Site works

Excavation, compaction, drainage and disposal. This is the part that varies most between two "identical" driveways, and the part cheap quotes quietly leave out.

CONCRETE DRIVEWAY COSTS IN MELBOURNE: WHAT'S LOCAL

Most "Melbourne" cost guides are generic Australian content with the city name in the title. A few things genuinely change the number here:

  • Council crossover rules vary. The crossover — the section between the road and your property boundary — generally needs council approval, and each council sets its own specification. In Wyndham, that's Wyndham City Council; requirements and fees differ from Casey, Bayside or Melton. Crossover works are usually quoted separately from the driveway itself.
  • The growth corridors are new-build territory. Across Werribee, Point Cook, Tarneit and Craigieburn, most driveways are first pours on new estate homes — clean sites, no demolition, often a more predictable price.
  • The established suburbs mean replacements. In older areas like Hoppers Crossing, you're more often removing a cracked 30-year-old slab first, which adds demolition, cartage and tip fees before a single cubic metre of concrete is poured.
  • Melbourne's weather affects curing. Cold or wet months slow the cure, and exposed aggregate in particular depends on washing back the surface at exactly the right moment — winter pours need more care, not more money, but they do need the right crew.
  • Seasonal demand moves labour rates. Spring and summer are peak season for outdoor concreting across Melbourne.

HOW TO WORK OUT YOUR OWN ESTIMATE

  1. Measure the length × width of the driveway in metres to get your area in m².
  2. Multiply the area by a per-m² rate from the table above, matched to the finish you want.
  3. Add for site prep, old-driveway removal, slope, access and crossover works if they apply.

Example: a 4m × 10m driveway is 40m². At $110/m² for plain concrete, that's about $4,400 before site-specific costs.

Treat this as a budget range, not a quote. Nobody can price a driveway accurately without seeing the site — which is why we do free on-site measures.

IS A CONCRETE DRIVEWAY WORTH IT?

Concrete costs more upfront than gravel or asphalt, and less than most paver installations. Where it wins is over time: a properly laid concrete driveway typically lasts 25–40 years with minimal maintenance, and it doesn't need the resealing cycle asphalt does. Cost per year of life is where concrete makes sense.

CONCRETE VS OTHER DRIVEWAY MATERIALS

MaterialCost per m²LifespanMaintenance
Concrete$70 – $20025–40 yrsMinimal
AsphaltLower15–25 yrsReseal every 2–5 yrs
Pavers / brickComparable–higher30–50 yrsRe-levelling, weeding
GravelLowestOngoingRegular topping up, migrates

Concrete's case isn't the lowest upfront price — it's cost per year of life. Asphalt is cheaper to lay and needs resealing every few years; gravel is cheapest and needs constant attention; pavers last well but individual units settle and need re-levelling.

MAINTENANCE AND LONG-TERM COST

Concrete is low-maintenance, not no-maintenance. Washing it down and occasional weeding of joints is most of it. Decorative and exposed aggregate finishes should be resealed every few years to protect the surface and keep the colour rich. Fine surface cracking is normal; structural cracking almost always traces back to a poorly compacted base or missing reinforcement — not the concrete itself.

Get Free Quote Now

FAQ

How much does a concrete driveway cost per m² in Melbourne?

Plain concrete typically runs $70–$130 per square metre, and decorative finishes like exposed aggregate $100–$200+ per square metre. The final figure depends on site prep, access, slope and whether an old driveway needs removing.

How much is a 40m² concrete driveway?

Roughly $2,800–$5,200 for plain concrete, or around $4,000–$7,200 for exposed aggregate, before site-specific costs like excavation, removal or crossover works.

Why is exposed aggregate more expensive?

It takes more labour and specialist timing — the surface is washed back at exactly the right point in the cure to reveal the stone — plus the decorative aggregate itself and a sealing step. Expect roughly 40–60% above plain concrete.

Does the quote include removing my old driveway?

Sometimes, sometimes not — it’s the most common hidden cost. Always ask whether demolition and removal are included or quoted separately.

Do I need council approval?


A new crossover onto the road generally needs council approval. A driveway on your own property often doesn’t. Requirements vary by council, and we’ll flag what your job needs before we start.

How long does a concrete driveway last?

25–40 years with minimal maintenance when it’s laid on a properly compacted base with correct reinforcement. Decorative finishes last just as long when sealed.

Can I get an exact price online?

No — and be wary of anyone who gives you one. Slope, access, base condition and removal all move the number. The only accurate price is an on-site measure, which we do free.

    Most \"Melbourne\" cost guides are generic Australian content with the city name in the title. A few things genuinely change the number here:<\/p>

    • Council crossover rules vary.<\/strong> The crossover \u2014 the section between the road and your property boundary \u2014 generally needs council approval, and each council sets its own specification. In Wyndham, that's Wyndham City Council<\/strong>; requirements and fees differ from Casey, Bayside or Melton. Crossover works are usually quoted separately from the driveway itself.<\/li>
    • The growth corridors are new-build territory.<\/strong> Across Werribee<\/a>, Point Cook<\/a>, Tarneit and Craigieburn, most driveways are first pours on new estate homes \u2014 clean sites, no demolition, often a more predictable price.<\/li>
    • The established suburbs mean replacements.<\/strong> In older areas like Hoppers Crossing, you're more often removing a cracked 30-year-old slab first, which adds demolition, cartage and tip fees before a single cubic metre of concrete is poured.<\/li>
    • Melbourne's weather affects curing.<\/strong> Cold or wet months slow the cure, and exposed aggregate in particular depends on washing back the surface at exactly the right moment \u2014 winter pours need more care, not more money, but they do need the right crew.<\/li>
    • Seasonal demand moves labour rates.<\/strong> Spring and summer are peak season for outdoor concreting across item.title: What Wyndham Council Actually Requires for a Vehicle Crossing (2026)
item.dc:creator: Admin-iU1Tj
item.content:encoded:
What Wyndham Council Actually Requires for a Vehicle Crossing (2026)

The Short Answer

If you want a new driveway crossover in Werribee, Point Cook, Tarneit, Hoppers Crossing or anywhere else in Wyndham, you need written consent from Wyndham City Council before any work starts. Not after. Not "we'll sort it later."

Five things most people don't find out until it's too late:

  1. You must apply at least 20 business days before works begin.
  2. Fees range from $102.60 to $737.01, depending on what you're touching and the speed limit of the road.
  3. Where there's a footpath, the crossing must be plain concrete — decorative finishes, colour pigment and pavers are not permitted.
  4. You need to give Council 24 hours' notice for a pre-pour inspection.
  5. Removing a street tree to fit your crossover starts at a $379.50 tree compensation fee, and mature trees generally won't be approved at all.

That last one about plain concrete surprises almost everyone. You can have exposed aggregate up your driveway. You can't carry it across the footpath.

How I put this together

I went through Wyndham City Council's own documentation rather than repeating what other sites say: the current Get consent for works on a road reserve page and its published fee schedule, the Community Amenity Local Law (2023), and Council's works specification document for vehicle crossings. Everything below is sourced from those. Where a figure comes from an older Council specification document, I've flagged it — Council updates specs and fees, so treat this as a map, not a substitute for their current paperwork.

What is a vehicle crossing? ​

The vehicle crossing — also called a crossover, or a layback where it meets the kerb — is the section of concrete between the road and your property boundary. It crosses the road reserve: Council's land, not yours.
Council defines the road reserve as the land between property boundaries covering the footpath, nature strip, kerb and channel, road shoulder and roadway.
That's the key point. Your driveway is yours. The crossover isn't. It sits on Council land, which is why they set the specification, inspect the works, and decide what finish is acceptable.

Residential vs industrial crossovers

A standard residential crossover is built for cars. If you need to accommodate a truck or heavy vehicle on a residential property, Council may require a suitable industrial crossover as part of a planning permit process — a heavier construction with different specifications. Don't assume a standard crossover will do.

Do you need Council consent for a vehicle crossing?

Yes. The Community Amenity Local Law (2023) is direct about it: a person must not, without authorisation from Council, construct, remove, alter, or relocate any vehicle crossing.

Construct, remove, alter or relocate. Widening an existing crossover counts. So does replacing one.

The Local Law also puts ongoing obligations on you as the owner:

  • Maintain the crossing in good condition
  • Align it with your internal driveway
  • Ensure vehicles only enter the property across a properly constructed crossing

Once it's built to Council specification, ongoing maintenance and upkeep becomes the owner's responsibility — not Council's. If it cracks or sinks in ten years, that's your bill.

Building new in Tarneit, Point Cook or Manor Lakes

This is where a lot of Wyndham homeowners get confused, so it's worth separating out.

In the growth estates, the crossover is usually part of the new build, not a later retrofit. That changes who does what:

  • If your crossover is part of a planning permit, your application needs to include a copy of the endorsed plan (not the permit itself).
  • The builder often handles the crossover as part of the build contract. Check your contract before you assume — it's a common gap, and a common assumption that turns out to be wrong.
  • The crossover location is frequently set by the endorsed plan, so you may have less freedom to move it than you'd think.

If you're buying an established home in Werribee or Hoppers Crossing and adding or replacing a crossover, none of that applies — you're the applicant, and everything in this article is on you.

Temporary vehicle crossings during construction

Less well known, and it catches builders and owner-builders out.

Under the Local Law, anyone in charge of a building site — or driving a vehicle onto one — must ensure entry only takes place across a properly constructed permanent or temporary vehicle crossing, unless Council permits otherwise.

So you can't just run trucks across the nature strip and kerb during the build and fix it later. If you damage Council assets doing it, you're into asset protection territory and reinstatement at your cost.

What you have to submit to Wyndham City Council

For a vehicle crossover, Council asks for an aerial image or diagram of your property frontage showing where the proposed crossover goes. That diagram needs to show:

  • all existing infrastructure — trees, drainage pits
  • clearance measurements between the crossover and that infrastructure

If your crossover relates to a current planning permit, include a copy of the endorsed plan. You don't need to include the permit itself.

Making a preliminary enquiry? You don't need to name your works manager or contractor yet.

Applications go through Council's online consent portal, linked from their road reserve consent page.

Vehicle crossing consent fees in Wyndham (2026)

Work on an area larger than 8.5m²

Road speed limit Affecting roadway, kerb & channel, road shoulder or footpath Nature strip (soil) only
50km/h or less $401.85 $102.60
More than 51km/h $737.01 $401.85

Work on an area smaller than 8.5m²

Road type Affecting roadway, kerb & channel, road shoulder or footpath Nature strip (soil) only
All roads $159.03 $102.60

A standard residential crossover in a 50km/h street, touching the footpath and kerb, lands at $401.85. That's the number most Wyndham homeowners are looking at.

Note this is the consent fee only — it's not the cost of the concreting work, and it doesn't include any tree compensation fee.

Wyndham's vehicle crossing design rules

These come from Council's works specification document. Confirm the current version with Council before you design anything around them.

Plain concrete only where there's a footpath

Decorative concrete finishes — with or without colouring pigment — and block paving using brick, stone or concrete interlocking pavers are not permitted. If you're planning exposed aggregate, stencil, coloured or honed concrete, it stops at the property boundary.

Clearances and sight lines

A crossing needs to be a minimum of 9 metres clear of the nearest intersection, and 3.0 metres clear of other assets. These aren't arbitrary — they exist to preserve sight lines for traffic and pedestrians.

Second crossovers

A second crossover is only approved where there's a minimum of 7 metres between the existing and the new crossover (to preserve on-street parking), and the property meets a minimum frontage requirement.

Crossover width

A crossing wider than 3.5m is only permitted where it's not possible to access the property otherwise.

Inspections, compaction testing and delivery dockets

This is where the job gets more involved than "pour some concrete."

  • 24 hours' notice to Council's Maintenance Depot for an inspection before the pour
  • Compaction tests carried out by NATA-registered personnel, with a copy of the results kept on site
  • Delivery dockets for all materials — Council's inspector will ask for them during inspection
  • The consent must be available for inspection by a Council officer at any time

If your concreter hasn't mentioned any of this, that's worth a conversation before they start. A crossover isn't the same job as a driveway — the subgrade preparation, compaction testing and inspection sequence are Council's call, not the contractor's.

Street trees and tree compensation fees

If a street tree is in the way, it triggers a separate investigation by Council's Urban Spaces & Council Works department.

If removal is approved, there's a tree compensation fee starting at $379.50 (incl. GST), scaling with the tree's height and age.

If it's not approved, you're told to submit a new proposal of works that avoids the tree. And removal of mature trees is strictly prohibited — approval will not be granted.

So the honest advice: design the crossover around the tree from the start. Assume you're not getting it removed.

How long does vehicle crossing consent take?

Council asks for 20 business days' notice minimum. That's four working weeks before you touch anything — and that's the application lead time, not an approval guarantee.

Add the pre-pour inspection booking (24 hours' notice), and any back-and-forth if your diagram is missing clearances or your finish isn't compliant.

Plan for at least a month between deciding you want a crossover and having anyone on site. In practice, longer if a tree or a planning permit is involved.

Why crossover applications get rejected

Based on what Council asks for, the failure points are predictable:

  • Diagram missing existing infrastructure or clearance measurements
  • Proposed crossover under 9m from an intersection
  • Second crossover without 7m separation from the existing one
  • Width over 3.5m without justification
  • Decorative, coloured or paved finish proposed across the footpath
  • A street tree in the way with no alternative design
  • Starting work before consent is issued

That last one is the expensive one. Building without authorisation breaches the Local Law, and a non-compliant crossing can be required to be removed and rebuilt — at your cost.

Related Wyndham permits you might also need

A crossover rarely sits alone. Depending on your job, you may also be dealing with:

  • Asset protection — protecting Council assets (kerb, footpath, drainage) during building works, and reinstating any damage
  • Legal point of discharge — where your stormwater is legally allowed to go
  • Build over easement — if your works cross an easement
  • Planning permit — for new developments, where the crossover appears on the endorsed plan

Getting your Wyndham crossover right the first time

The crossover is the one part of your driveway where Council decides what's acceptable — the specification, the compaction, the inspection and the finish. Get it wrong and you're rebuilding it at your own cost.

If you're planning a new driveway in Werribee, Point Cook, Tarneit or Hoppers Crossing and want the crossover done to Council spec, get a free on-site quote from E&T Co — or read our guide to concrete driveways in Melbourne.

Fees, specifications and requirements sourced from Wyndham City Council and the Community Amenity Local Law (2023), correct at the time of writing. Council fees and specifications change — always confirm current requirements directly with Wyndham City Council on 1300 023 411 before starting works. This article is general information, not a substitute for Council's own documentation.

FAQ

Do I need Council consent to replace an existing crossover in Wyndham?

Yes. The Community Amenity Local Law (2023) covers constructing, removing, altering or relocating a vehicle crossing. Replacement is covered.

How much does vehicle crossing consent cost in Wyndham?

Between $102.60 and $737.01 depending on the area and road speed limit. A typical residential crossover affecting the footpath on a 50km/h road is $401.85. That’s the consent fee only, not the construction cost.

Can I have exposed aggregate or coloured concrete on my crossover?

Not where a footpath is present. Council’s specification requires plain concrete and doesn’t permit decorative finishes, colour pigment or pavers across the crossing. Your driveway inside the property boundary is a different story.

How long does it take to get consent?

Apply at least 20 business days before works start. Allow longer if a tree or planning permit is involved.

Who applies — me or my concreter?

The application relates to your property, and the owner carries the Local Law obligations. Many concreters will help prepare the diagram, but confirm with Council who they’ll accept as applicant for your job.

Is the crossover included in my new build contract?

Often, in the growth estates — but check your contract rather than assuming. It’s a common gap.

Who maintains the crossover once it's built?

You do. Once constructed to Council specification, ongoing maintenance and upkeep is the property owner’s responsibility.

Can I remove a street tree to fit my driveway?

Possibly, if it’s not mature — but it triggers a separate Council investigation and a tree compensation fee starting at $379.50. Mature tree removal is prohibited.

How wide can my crossover be?

Standard is up to 3.5m. Wider is only permitted where access isn’t otherwise possible.

The vehicle crossing — also called a crossover, or a layback where it meets the kerb — is the section of concrete between the road and your property boundary. It crosses the road reserve: Council's land, not yours.
Council defines the road reserve as the land between property boundaries covering the footpath, nature strip, kerb and channel, road shoulder and roadway.
That's the key point. Your driveway is yours. The crossover isn't. It sits on Council land, which is why they set the specification, inspect the works, and decide what finish is acceptable.

A standard residential crossover is built for cars. If you need to accommodate a truck or heavy vehicle on a residential property, Council may require a suitable industrial crossover as part of a planning permit process — a heavier construction with different specifications. Don't assume a standard crossover will do.

Yes. The Community Amenity Local Law (2023) is direct about it: a person must not, without authorisation from Council, construct, remove, alter, or relocate any vehicle crossing.

Construct, remove, alter or relocate. Widening an existing crossover counts. So does replacing one.

The Local Law also puts ongoing obligations on you as the owner:

  • Maintain the crossing in good condition
  • Align it with your internal driveway
  • Ensure vehicles only enter the property across a properly constructed crossing

Once it's built to Council specification, ongoing maintenance and upkeep becomes the owner's responsibility — not Council's. If it cracks or sinks in ten years, that's your bill.

This is where a lot of Wyndham homeowners get confused, so it's worth separating out.

In the growth estates, the crossover is usually part of the new build, not a later retrofit. That changes who does what:

  • If your crossover is part of a planning permit, your application needs to include a copy of the endorsed plan (not the permit itself).
  • The builder often handles the crossover as part of the build contract. Check your contract before you assume — it's a common gap, and a common assumption that turns out to be wrong.
  • The crossover location is frequently set by the endorsed plan, so you may have less freedom to move it than you'd think.

If you're buying an established home in Werribee or Hoppers Crossing and adding or replacing a crossover, none of that applies — you're the applicant, and everything in this article is on you.

Less well known, and it catches builders and owner-builders out.

Under the Local Law, anyone in charge of a building site — or driving a vehicle onto one — must ensure entry only takes place across a properly constructed permanent or temporary vehicle crossing, unless Council permits otherwise.

So you can't just run trucks across the nature strip and kerb during the build and fix it later. If you damage Council assets doing it, you're into asset protection territory and reinstatement at your cost.

For a vehicle crossover, Council asks for an aerial image or diagram of your property frontage showing where the proposed crossover goes. That diagram needs to show:

  • all existing infrastructure — trees, drainage pits
  • clearance measurements between the crossover and that infrastructure

If your crossover relates to a current planning permit, include a copy of the endorsed plan. You don't need to include the permit itself.

Making a preliminary enquiry? You don't need to name your works manager or contractor yet.

Applications go through Council's online consent portal, linked from their road reserve consent page.

A crossing needs to be a minimum of 9 metres clear of the nearest intersection, and 3.0 metres clear of other assets. These aren't arbitrary — they exist to preserve sight lines for traffic and pedestrians.

This is where the job gets more involved than "pour some concrete."

  • 24 hours' notice to Council's Maintenance Depot for an inspection before the pour
  • Compaction tests carried out by NATA-registered personnel, with a copy of the results kept on site
  • Delivery dockets for all materials — Council's inspector will ask for them during inspection
  • The consent must be available for inspection by a Council officer at any time

If your concreter hasn't mentioned any of this, that's worth a conversation before they start. A crossover isn't the same job as a driveway — the subgrade preparation, compaction testing and inspection sequence are Council's call, not the contractor's.

If a street tree is in the way, it triggers a separate investigation by Council's Urban Spaces & Council Works department.

If removal is approved, there's a tree compensation fee starting at $379.50 (incl. GST), scaling with the tree's height and age.

If it's not approved, you're told to submit a new proposal of works that avoids the tree. And removal of mature trees is strictly prohibited — approval will not be granted.

So the honest advice: design the crossover around the tree from the start. Assume you're not getting it removed.

Council asks for 20 business days' notice minimum. That's four working weeks before you touch anything — and that's the application lead time, not an approval guarantee.

Add the pre-pour inspection booking (24 hours' notice), and any back-and-forth if your diagram is missing clearances or your finish isn't compliant.

Plan for at least a month between deciding you want a crossover and having anyone on site. In practice, longer if a tree or a planning permit is involved.

Based on what Council asks for, the failure points are predictable:

  • Diagram missing existing infrastructure or clearance measurements
  • Proposed crossover under 9m from an intersection
  • Second crossover without 7m separation from the existing one
  • Width over 3.5m without justification
  • Decorative, coloured or paved finish proposed across the footpath
  • A street tree in the way with no alternative design
  • Starting work before consent is issued

That last one is the expensive one. Building without authorisation breaches the Local Law, and a non-compliant crossing can be required to be removed and rebuilt — at your cost.

A crossover rarely sits alone. Depending on your job, you may also be dealing with:

  • Asset protection — protecting Council assets (kerb, footpath, drainage) during building works, and reinstating any damage
  • Legal point of discharge — where your stormwater is legally allowed to go
  • Build over easement — if your works cross an easement
  • Planning permit — for new developments, where the crossover appears on the endorsed plan

If you're planning a new driveway in Werribee, Point Cook, Tarneit or Hoppers Crossing and want the crossover done to Council spec, get a free on-site quote from E&T Co — or read our guide to concrete driveways in Melbourne.

item.title: Coloured & Decorative Concrete Melbourne
item.dc:creator: Admin-iU1Tj
item.content:encoded:
Coloured & Decorative Concrete Melbourne​

Decorative concrete gives you the strength and low maintenance of a poured slab with a finish that lifts the look of the whole property. Instead of plain grey, the surface is coloured, textured or patterned — so a driveway, path or alfresco area becomes a feature rather than just a functional slab. We pour decorative concrete across Melbourne and the western suburbs, and we'll walk you through which finish suits your site, your budget and the way water needs to run off it.

Decorative concrete finishes we pour

Coloured concrete

Colour oxides are mixed through the pour (integral colour) or applied to the surface, giving a consistent tone right through the slab in shades like charcoal, sandstone, slate grey and terracotta. Because the colour is in the concrete rather than on top of it, it wears far better than a painted surface. It's the simplest way to move away from plain grey, and it pairs with most of the finishes below.

Stencil concrete

A removable pattern sheet is laid onto the wet concrete and a colour hardener applied over it, then lifted to leave crisp lines — mimicking pavers, brick, cobblestone or tile. Stencil is one of the most cost-effective decorative finishes, which is why it's popular on driveways in the western estates where homeowners want a patterned look without the price of stamped work.

Stamped (imprinted) concrete

Patterned mats are pressed into the wet surface to replicate natural stone, slate, cobblestone or timber. Stamped concrete gives the closest imitation of premium materials at a fraction of the cost of the real thing, and combined with colour oxides it can be fully customised. It's the higher end of the decorative range — more materials and finishing time — and it's a genuine feature finish for driveways and alfresco areas.

Honed & polished concrete

The non-slip finish makes it a common choice around pools.

Exposed aggregate

Technically the most popular decorative finish in Melbourne — the top layer of cement is removed to reveal the stone in the mix, leaving a textured, slip-resistant surface with real kerb appeal. We cover it in detail on our exposed aggregate page.

Choosing a finish that lasts, not just looks good

A decorative finish is only as good as the slab under it. Melbourne's western suburbs sit largely on reactive clay — Class M through to Class H — which swells and shrinks with the seasons and moves the ground beneath a driveway. A beautiful stencil or stamped surface laid over a poorly prepared base will still crack, and a crack through a patterned finish is far more obvious than through plain grey.

So the decorative choice sits on top of the fundamentals: a compacted crushed-rock sub-base, reinforcement held at the correct height, adequate thickness, control joints placed to let the slab move, and the right falls so water runs off rather than pooling. We price the prep and the finish together on a fixed, itemised quote — thickness, mesh, joints, finish and sealing — so you can see what you're paying for.

Sealing and maintenance

Most decorative finishes should be sealed to protect the colour and surface from Melbourne's weather and UV, and resealed every few years depending on traffic and exposure. Sealing deepens the colour on exposed aggregate and coloured concrete, and protects the pattern lines on stencil and stamped work. We'll set out the reseal timing for your chosen finish when we quote, so there are no surprises down the track.

Where a decorative finish stops — council crossovers

One thing worth knowing if you're planning a decorative driveway: the section that crosses onto the road — the vehicle crossover — usually has to be plain concrete where there's a footpath, under council rules. So your coloured, stencil or stamped finish runs up the driveway and stops at the property boundary. We handle the crossover consent as part of the job and set the job out so the transition looks deliberate.

item.title: Concreters Tarneit
item.dc:creator: Admin-iU1Tj
item.content:encoded:
Concreters Tarneit

Tarneit is one of the fastest-growing suburbs in Melbourne's west, which means a lot of brand-new homes needing driveways, slabs, paths and outdoor areas poured from scratch. But Tarneit comes with ground conditions that matter more here than almost anywhere else in Wyndham — and getting them wrong is why so many estate driveways crack within a few years.

Get Your FREE Quote Today Call us - 03 4427 9541

Our Services

Whatever the pour, we match you with concreters who do it every week.

Concrete Driveways

New driveways, replacements, crossovers

Exposed Aggregate

The premium textured, non-slip finish with real kerb appeal.

Concrete Slabs

Shed, garage, extension and house slabs fitted properly for your needs

Paths & Pathways

Footpaths, side access, garden paths

Patios & Alfresco

Outdoor entertaining areas

Coloured & Decorative

Coloured, stencil, honed finishes

Tarneit's soil is the reason driveways fail early

Much of the Tarneit, Truganina and Wyndham Vale belt is classified Class H reactive clay under AS 2870 — a step more reactive than the Class M ground common closer to the bay — with pockets of Class P sites where old agricultural fill has been built over. Reactive clay swells when wet and shrinks when it dries, and the more reactive the class, the more the ground moves under a slab through the seasons. (Here's why concrete cracks on reactive clay in detail.)

On Class H and P ground, a driveway laid straight onto dirt with mesh sitting on the base will crack — it's not a matter of if. Proper work here means a compacted crushed-rock sub-base, reinforcement held at the correct height on bar chairs (not thrown on the ground), adequate slab thickness, and control joints placed to let the concrete move without tearing. That's the difference between a driveway that lasts and one that's cracked before the warranty's up.

Drainage and falls near the creek corridors

Tarneit isn't uniformly flat. Much of the newer development around the Riverdale precinct runs down toward Davis Creek, Skeleton Creek and the Werribee River, so parts of the suburb carry subtle slopes and sit close to waterways. Combined with reactive clay, that makes water management critical — standing water against a slab drives the exact moisture changes that move the ground underneath it.

We set the correct falls (typically a 1–2% grade away from the house) and plan drainage so water runs off rather than pooling. On this ground that's a structural issue, not just a cosmetic one — poor drainage is one of the fastest ways to crack a driveway in Tarneit.

New estates we pour across in Tarneit

Most of our Tarneit work is new-build, on fresh estate lots across the suburb — estates like Newgate, Riverdale Village, Habitat on Davis Creek, The Grove, Haven, Marigold, Claremont Park and Creekstone, among many others still releasing land. Typical estate blocks run around 350–520m², with driveways in the 40–75m² range plus the council crossover.

One thing worth knowing on estate lots: the ground has usually been compacted and moved around by the building trades before the driveway stage, so the sub-base needs checking rather than assuming it's sound. We assess what's actually there before we pour, so the finished slab sits on a base that holds.

Driveway finishes for Tarneit homes

New estate homes are where decorative finishes earn their place, and they're popular across Tarneit. We pour plain concrete driveways, exposed aggregate for a textured, non-slip finish with real kerb appeal, and coloured and stencil finishes that lift the front of the house. Whatever the finish, it sits on the same properly prepared base — the surface is the look, the base is what makes it last.

Council crossovers in Tarneit

Every new driveway that meets the road needs a council-approved vehicle crossover before it's poured. It sits on Wyndham City Council land, comes with a consent fee and a lead time, and has to be plain concrete where there's a footpath — so a decorative driveway finish stops at the property boundary. We handle that consent as part of the job, built to council spec, so you're not chasing paperwork yourself.

AREAS WE COVER AROUND TARNEIT

We service Werribee and the surrounding Wyndham suburbs, including Werribee South, Wyndham Vale, Hoppers Crossing, Point Cook, Tarneit and Truganina.

Planning Concrete Work in Tarneit?

Get Your FREE Quote Today

FAQ

Do you service all of Tarneit?

Yes — we pour across the whole suburb and the surrounding Wyndham area, including the newer estates north and south of Davis Creek and the Riverdale precinct.

How much does a concrete driveway cost in Tarneit?

It depends on size, finish and site access. Plain concrete sits at the lower end; exposed aggregate and decorative finishes cost more. On reactive clay, proper base prep is part of the price — it’s what stops the slab cracking. We give a fixed price after an on-site measure.

Do I need council approval for my driveway in Tarneit?

The driveway on your own property generally doesn’t, but the crossover onto the road does — it needs Wyndham City Council consent before it’s poured. We handle that as part of the job.

Much of the Tarneit, Truganina and Wyndham Vale belt is classified Class H<\/strong> reactive clay under AS 2870 \u2014 a step more reactive than the Class M ground common closer to the bay \u2014 with pockets of Class P<\/strong> sites where old agricultural fill has been built over. Reactive clay swells when wet and shrinks when it dries, and the more reactive the class, the more the ground moves under a slab through the seasons. (Here's why concrete cracks on reactive clay<\/a> in detail.)<\/p>

On Class H and P ground, a driveway laid straight onto dirt with mesh sitting on the base will crack \u2014 it's not a matter of if. Proper work here means a compacted crushed-rock sub-base, reinforcement held at the correct height on bar chairs (not thrown on the ground), adequate slab thickness, and control joints placed to let the concrete move without tearing. That's the difference between a driveway that lasts and one that's cracked before the warranty's Tarneit isn't uniformly flat. Much of the newer development around the Riverdale precinct runs down toward Davis Creek, Skeleton Creek and the Werribee River<\/strong>, so parts of the suburb carry subtle slopes and sit close to waterways. Combined with reactive clay, that makes water management critical \u2014 standing water against a slab drives the exact moisture changes that move the ground underneath it.<\/p>\n

We set the correct falls (typically a 1\u20132% grade away from the house) and plan drainage so water runs off rather than pooling. On this ground that's a structural issue, not just a cosmetic one \u2014 poor drainage is one of the fastest ways to crack a driveway in Tarneit.<\/p>","typography_typography":"custom","typography_font_family":"Poppins","typography_font_weight":"400","_padding":{"unit":"px","top":"30","right":"0","bottom":"0","left":"0","isLinked":false},"__globals__":{"text_color":"globals\/colors?id=astglobalcolor2"}},"elements":[],"widgetType":"text-editor"}],"isInner":false,"styles":{"e-c4e3125-5b7a4c3":{"id":"e-c4e3125-5b7a4c3","label":"local","type":"class","variants":[{"meta":{"breakpoint":"desktop","state":null},"props":{"padding":{"$$type":"dimensions","value":{"block-start":{"$$type":"size","value":{"size":30,"unit":"px"}}}},"flex-direction":{"$$type":"string","value":"column"}},"custom_css":null}]}},"interactions":[],"editor_settings":[],"version":"0.0"}],"isInner":false},{"id":"aad755d","elType":"e-flexbox","settings":{"classes":{"$$type":"classes","value":["e-aad755d-d34d1f4"]}},"elements":[{"id":"6cf076a","elType":"widget","settings":{"classes":{"$$type":"classes","value":["e-6cf076a-87e7a36"]},"title":{"$$type":"html-v3","value":{"content":{"$$type":"string","value":"New estates we pour across in Tarneit"},"children":[]}},"link":{"$$type":"link","value":{"isTargetBlank":null}}},"elements":[],"widgetType":"e-heading","styles":{"e-6cf076a-87e7a36":{"id":"e-6cf076a-87e7a36","label":"local","type":"class","variants":[{"meta":{"breakpoint":"desktop","state":null},"props":{"font-family":{"$$type":"font-family","value":"Poppins"},"font-weight":{"$$type":"string","value":"300"},"font-size":{"$$type":"size","value":{"size":40,"unit":"px"}},"text-align":{"$$type":"string","value":"center"}},"custom_css":null}]}},"interactions":[],"editor_settings":[],"version":"0.0"},{"id":"acd7626","elType":"widget","settings":{"editor":"

item.title: Concreters Hoppers Crossing
item.dc:creator: Admin-iU1Tj
item.content:encoded:
Concreters Hoppers Crossing

Hoppers Crossing is one of the oldest suburbs in Wyndham — and unlike the new estates around it, it's fully built out. Most homes here went up between the 1970s and 1990s, which means the concrete is doing the same. Original driveways, paths and slabs from that era are now 30 to 50 years old, cracking, lifting and past their use-by date. We handle both sides of that: replacing tired old concrete on established Hoppers Crossing homes, and pouring new work for knockdown-rebuilds and extensions. Free on-site, fixed-price quotes.

Get Your FREE Quote Today Call us - 03 4427 9541

Our Services

Whatever the pour, we match you with concreters who do it every week.

Concrete Driveways

New driveways, replacements, crossovers

Exposed Aggregate

The premium textured, non-slip finish with real kerb appeal.

Concrete Slabs

Shed, garage, extension and house slabs fitted properly for your needs

Paths & Pathways

Footpaths, side access, garden paths

Patios & Alfresco

Outdoor entertaining areas

Coloured & Decorative

Coloured, stencil, honed finishes

Concreting for an established suburb, not a new estate

Aging concrete on 1970s-90s homes

Hoppers Crossing grew fastest between the early 1970s and the 1990s, and it's now fully built out — there's no new estate land left. That changes the concreting work here. Where Tarneit and Point Cook are about pouring driveways on fresh estate lots, Hoppers Crossing is largely about replacing concrete that's reached the end of its life: original driveways that have cracked and lifted, paths that have become trip hazards, and slabs poured to 1980s standards that never handled the reactive clay properly in the first place.

Knockdown-rebuilds and renovations

The other half of the work is the suburb's steady turnover. With no new land, growth comes from knockdown-rebuilds and renovations of the existing stock — which means new driveways, extension slabs and outdoor areas going in as older homes are updated. We cover both: tearing out and replacing tired concrete, and pouring fresh work for a rebuild or an extension.

The same reactive clay — with older concrete on top of it

Hoppers Crossing sits on the same reactive clay that runs under Werribee and the rest of the western plains — flat volcanic ground, classified Class M to Class H under AS 2870, that swells when wet and shrinks when it dries. It's the reason so much of the suburb's original concrete has cracked: a lot of it was poured decades ago on bases that weren't prepared for how much this ground moves. That's exactly why a like-for-like replacement isn't the answer... (Here's why concrete cracks on reactive clay, and how the base controls it.)

That's exactly why a like-for-like replacement isn't the answer — repouring a driveway the same way it was done in 1985 just repeats the failure. We rebuild the base properly: a compacted crushed-rock sub-base, reinforcement held at the correct height on bar chairs, adequate slab thickness, control joints placed to let the slab move, and the right falls so water runs off rather than pooling. On this ground, the base is what decides whether the new concrete lasts 5 years or 40.

Crossovers on older Hoppers Crossing properties

On established homes, the vehicle crossover — where the driveway meets the road — is often the original one, decades old and cracked. If you're replacing your driveway, it's the natural time to redo the crossover too. It sits on council land, needs Wyndham City Council consent, comes with a fee and a lead time, and has to be plain concrete where there's a footpath. We handle that consent as part of the job so you're not chasing council yourself.

Concreting across Hoppers Crossing and nearby

We're based in Werribee, five minutes away, so we're in Hoppers Crossing regularly for quotes and work. We also service Werribee, Point Cook, Tarneit and the surrounding Wyndham suburbs. For the full range of what we do, see our concreters Melbourne page.

Get Your FREE Quote Today

FAQ

Do you replace old cracked driveways?

Yes — replacement is most of what we do in Hoppers Crossing, given the suburb’s older housing. We break out the old driveway, rebuild the base properly for the reactive clay, and repour so the new one actually lasts rather than cracking again.

Why did my original driveway crack?

Almost always a base problem. Much of Hoppers Crossing’s original concrete was poured decades ago on bases that weren’t built for how much the local reactive clay moves. A like-for-like repour repeats the mistake — the fix is rebuilding the base correctly.

Can you redo my crossover at the same time?

Yes, and it’s the sensible time to do it. If your driveway’s being replaced, redoing the aging crossover in the same job saves a second setup. It needs Wyndham Council consent, which we handle.

How much does a new driveway cost in Hoppers Crossing?

It depends on size, finish, and whether the old driveway needs removing first. Removal and base rebuild are part of the price on a replacement. We give a fixed on-site quote after measuring.

Aging concrete on 1970s-90s homes<\/span><\/h3>\n

Hoppers Crossing grew fastest between the early 1970s and the 1990s, and it's now fully built out \u2014 there's no new estate land left. That changes the concreting work here. Where Tarneit and Point Cook are about pouring driveways on fresh estate lots, Hoppers Crossing is largely about replacing concrete that's reached the end of its life<\/strong>: original driveways that have cracked and lifted, paths that have become trip hazards, and slabs poured to 1980s standards that never handled the reactive clay properly in the first place.<\/p>\n

Knockdown-rebuilds and renovations<\/h3>\n

The other half of the work is the suburb's steady turnover. Concreters Truganina

Truganina is one of Melbourne's fastest-growing western suburbs — home to more than 36,000 people and still expanding across new estates on both the Wyndham and Melton sides of the boundary. That means a steady stream of brand-new homes needing driveways, slabs, paths and outdoor areas poured from scratch. But Truganina's volcanic clay is some of the most reactive ground in the west, and it's the single biggest reason estate driveways and slabs crack within a few years. We pour concrete built for that ground, not against it. Free on-site, fixed-price quotes.

Get Your FREE Quote Today Call us - 03 4427 9541

Our Services

Whatever the pour, we match you with concreters who do it every week.

Concrete Driveways

New driveways, replacements, crossovers

Exposed Aggregate

The premium textured, non-slip finish with real kerb appeal.

Concrete Slabs

Shed, garage, extension and house slabs fitted properly for your needs

Paths & Pathways

Footpaths, side access, garden paths

Patios & Alfresco

Outdoor entertaining areas

Coloured & Decorative

Coloured, stencil, honed finishes

Truganina's reactive clay and the slab-heave problem

h3>Some of the most reactive ground in the west

Truganina sits on flat volcanic plains with highly reactive clay — classified toward the Class H end under AS 2870. This ground swells when wet and shrinks when it dries, and the more reactive it is, the more it moves under a slab through the seasons. Local building inspectors flag Truganina specifically for the risk: poor site drainage on this clay leads to slab heave, where the ground lifts unevenly and cracks driveways, paths and floor slabs. Here's why concrete cracks on reactive clay in detail.)

Why estate driveways here crack early

On this ground, a driveway laid straight onto dirt with mesh sitting on the base will crack — it's not a matter of if. Proper work in Truganina means a compacted crushed-rock sub-base, reinforcement held at the correct height on bar chairs (not thrown on the ground), adequate slab thickness, control joints placed to let the concrete move, and — critically here — drainage and falls that keep water away from the slab. On reactive clay, poor drainage is what drives the moisture swings that heave and crack the concrete. Get the base and the falls right and the driveway lasts.

New estates across Truganina

Most of our Truganina work is new-build, on fresh estate lots. The suburb is being built out across dozens of estates — Mount Atkinson, Allura, Elysian, Grandview, Botanical and Westbrook among many others still releasing land. Typical estate blocks need a driveway, a shed or garage slab, paths and often an alfresco area, all poured from scratch.

One thing worth knowing on estate lots: the ground has usually been cut, filled and compacted by the building trades before the driveway stage, so the sub-base needs checking rather than assuming it's sound — especially on fill. We assess what's actually under the slab before we pour, because on Truganina's clay the base is what decides whether the concrete holds.

Concrete for Truganina's industrial and commercial precincts

Truganina isn't only residential — it's one of Wyndham's major industrial and logistics hubs, with warehousing and manufacturing across the suburb. That means demand for larger commercial and heavy-duty concrete work too: warehouse and factory slabs, hardstand areas, loading zones and heavy-vehicle driveways that have to carry far more load than a home driveway. These jobs need thicker slabs, engineered reinforcement and a base built for the traffic. If you've got a commercial pour in the Truganina precinct, we can quote it alongside the residential work.

Council crossovers in Truganina

Every new driveway that meets the road needs a council-approved vehicle crossover before it's poured. On the Wyndham side of Truganina that's Wyndham City Council; the northern pocket falls under Melton. Either way the crossover sits on council land, comes with a consent fee and a lead time, and has to be plain concrete where there's a footpath — so a decorative driveway finish stops at the boundary. We handle the consent as part of the job so you're not chasing council yourself.

s

Concreting across Truganina and nearby

We pour across Truganina and the surrounding Wyndham suburbs, including Tarneit, Werribee, Point Cook and Hoppers Crossing. For the full range of what we do, see our concreters Melbourne page.

Get Your FREE Quote Today

FAQ

Why does concrete crack so much in Truganina?

The volcanic clay here is highly reactive — it swells and shrinks with the seasons and, with poor drainage, causes slab heave. Concrete poured on a base that isn’t built for that movement cracks early. The fix is proper base prep and drainage, which is what we build for.

Do you pour on new estate lots?

Yes — most of our Truganina work is new-build across the estates. We check the sub-base first, because estate lots are often on cut-and-fill ground that needs verifying before we pour.

Do you do commercial and warehouse slabs?

Yes. Truganina’s a major industrial precinct, and we pour larger commercial slabs, hardstand and heavy-vehicle areas alongside residential work. These need thicker slabs and engineered reinforcement, which we quote per job.

How much does a concrete driveway cost in Truganina?

It depends on size, finish and site access. Plain concrete is at the lower end; exposed aggregate and decorative finishes cost more. Proper base prep for the reactive clay is part of the price. We give a fixed on-site quote.

h3>Some of the most reactive ground in the west<\/p>

Truganina sits on flat volcanic plains with highly reactive clay<\/strong> \u2014 classified toward the Class H end under AS 2870. This ground swells when wet and shrinks when it dries, and the more reactive it is, the more it moves under a slab through the seasons. Local building inspectors flag Truganina specifically for the risk: poor site drainage on this clay leads to slab heave<\/strong>, where the ground lifts unevenly and cracks driveways, paths and floor slabs. Here's why concrete cracks on reactive clay<\/a> in detail.)<\/p>

Why estate driveways here crack early<\/h3>

On this ground, a driveway laid straight onto dirt with mesh sitting on the base will crack \u2014 it's not a matter of if. Proper work in Truganina means a compacted crushed-rock sub-base, reinforcement held at the correct height on bar chairs (not thrown on the ground), adequate slab thickness, control joints placed to let the concrete move, and \u2014 critically here \u2014 drainage and falls that keep water away from the slab. On reactive clay, poor drainage is what drives the moisture swings that heave and crack the concrete. Get the base and the falls right and the driveway lasts.<\/p>","typography_typography":"custom","typography_font_family":"Poppins","typography_font_weight":"400","__globals__":{"text_color":"globals\/colors?id=astglobalcolor2"}},"elements":[],"widgetType":"text-editor"}],"isInner":true}],"isInner":true}],"isInner":false},{"id":"1dd2110e","elType":"container","settings":{"container_type":"grid","grid_columns_grid":{"unit":"fr","size":"2"},"grid_rows_grid":{"unit":"fr","size":"1"},"grid_rows_grid_mobile":{"unit":"fr","size":"1"}},"elements":[{"id":"7f4d47bb","elType":"container","settings":{"content_width":"full"},"elements":[{"id":"2e6d2ce5","elType":"widget","settings":{"classes":{"$$type":"classes","value":["e-2e6d2ce5-1293310"]},"title":{"$$type":"html-v3","value":{"content":{"$$type":"string","value":"New estates across Truganina"},"children":[]}},"link":{"$$type":"link","value":{"isTargetBlank":null}}},"elements":[],"widgetType":"e-heading","styles":{"e-2e6d2ce5-1293310":{"id":"e-2e6d2ce5-1293310","label":"local","type":"class","variants":[{"meta":{"breakpoint":"desktop","state":null},"props":{"font-family":{"$$type":"font-family","value":"Poppins"},"font-weight":{"$$type":"string","value":"400"},"font-size":{"$$type":"size","value":{"size":30,"unit":"px"}}},"custom_css":null}]}},"interactions":[],"editor_settings":[],"version":"0.0"},{"id":"31c0b970","elType":"widget","settings":{"editor":"

Most of our Truganina work is new-build, on fresh estate lots. The suburb is being built out across dozens of estates \u2014 Mount Atkinson, Allura, Elysian, Grandview, Botanical and Westbrook<\/strong> among many others still releasing land. Typical estate blocks need a driveway, a shed or garage slab, paths and often an alfresco area, all poured from scratch.<\/p>\n

One thing worth knowing on estate lots: the ground has usually been cut, filled and compacted by the building trades before the driveway stage, so the sub-base needs checking rather than assuming it's sound \u2014 especially on fill. We assess what's actually under the slab before we pour, because on Truganina's clay the base is what decides whether the concrete
